hook: The mystery man of numbers, whose theorem every student learns.

pages.x: Pythagoras was born on the Greek island of Samos around 570 BC. Stories say he travelled to Egypt and Babylon to learn from their priests. Around 530 BC, fleeing the tyrant of Samos, he settled in Croton, a Greek city in southern Italy.

In Croton he gathered a community of followers, men and women, who shared their property, studied in silence and believed that souls are reborn in new bodies. They would not eat beans. Once, a story says, he stopped a man beating a puppy, saying he recognised a dead friend's voice in its yelps.
In a right-angled triangle, the square on the longest side equals the squares on the other two sides added together: 3 squared plus 4 squared is 5 squared.
pages.fx: It is the most famous theorem in mathematics, used to work out distances on building sites, in maps and in GPS. Babylonians knew it 1,000 years earlier, but the Greeks are the first we know of to prove it.

pages.x: A legend says he heard hammers ringing in harmony in a smithy. He found that pleasing notes come from simple ratios: a string half as long sounds an octave higher.
pages.fx: The idea that nature follows mathematical rules is the foundation of physics. He is also said to have coined the words "philosophy" and "cosmos".

pages.t: Saved by beans? Killed by them
pages.x: When enemies set fire to the brotherhood's house in Croton, one story says, Pythagoras escaped but stopped at the edge of a bean field. Rather than trample the beans, he let his pursuers catch him. Another story says he starved himself in a temple. No one really knows.

Pythagoras wrote nothing, and legend has buried the real man. But his belief that "all is number", that the universe can be understood through mathematics, inspired Plato, Kepler and Newton and runs through all of modern science.
pts: Gave his name to the most famous theorem in mathematics
Taught that the universe follows numbers
